strengths: Directly resolves explicit open problems posed by Froese et al. at COLT'25 regarding the parameterized complexity of network verification (positivity/surjectivity) and Lipschitz constant computation, which is a clear and well-defined contribution.

The core reduction from MULTICOLORED CLIQUE is technically careful and clever, using Sidon sets to uniquely encode node/edge labels and 'spike'/'penalty' gadgets to enforce clique structure with input dimension scaling linearly with the clique size k -- this is the key technical difficulty that distinguishes parameterized hardness from ordinary NP-hardness reductions.

The results are comprehensive: they extend from basic positivity/surjectivity to zonotope (non-)containment (via an established duality), approximate maximization, and Lp-Lipschitz constant computation for a broad range of p, unifying several previously separate hardness results under one reduction technique.

ETH-based lower bounds are derived that match existing brute-force/enumeration algorithms, showing these naive approaches are essentially optimal, which is a stronger and more informative statement than plain NP-hardness.

The paper also contributes some positive/tractability results (poly-time L1 and FPT L∞ Lipschitz constant computation for input-convex networks, and a randomized FPT-approximation for zonotope norm maximization via subspace embeddings), giving a fuller complexity picture rather than only hardness.

Clear connections are drawn between disparate areas (ReLU network verification, zonotope containment, Lipschitz estimation), which is valuable for readers working in any one of these areas and highlights the paper's cross-disciplinary relevance.
Proofs appear rigorous and are supported with detailed appendices, and the main text is generally well organized with helpful illustrative figures.
weaknesses: The paper is purely theoretical with no experimental validation of any kind (acknowledged by the authors themselves as a limitation); for a general AI venue, this significantly narrows the immediate audience and practical impact even though the theory is solid.

The main proof technique (spike/penalty function gadgets reducing from Multicolored Clique) is a direct technical extension of constructions already used in Froese et al. (2025b); while the extensions (homogenization, scaling for Lipschitz constants) are nontrivial, the overall approach is incremental relative to that prior work rather than introducing a fundamentally new technique.

The central most interesting open question -- whether 2-LAYER RELU POSITIVITY is actually contained in W[1] (which would fully settle the parameterized complexity) -- remains unresolved, leaving the picture incomplete despite the paper's claim of 'settling the parameterized complexity almost completely.'

The scope is very narrow and specialized (parameterized complexity of specific ReLU network subproblems), which may appeal to a small niche of theoretical computer scientists rather than the broader AI/ML community typically targeted by a general top-tier AI conference.

Some of the positive results (e.g., ICNN tractability, FPT-approximation via subspace embeddings) are relatively minor additions with straightforward proofs built on existing results (e.g., Hertrich & Loho 2024, Cohen & Peng 2015), and the FPT-approximation runtime is admittedly worse than existing sampling-based results in the worst case, limiting their significance.

Discussion of practical implications for real-world verification tools/heuristics is thin; the conclusion largely restates that heuristics are 'required' without concrete guidance connecting the hardness results to practical network architectures or training procedures.

strengths: Resolves an explicitly posed open problem from COLT '25 (Froese et al.) regarding parameterized complexity of ReLU network verification, positivity, and zonotope containment, which is a clear and well-motivated contribution to the community.

The core reduction from MULTICOLORED CLIQUE is technically careful: the use of Sidon sets to encode node/edge labels so that spike and penalty functions interact correctly is a clever and non-trivial construction, and the authors clearly address the key technical difficulty (keeping input dimension linear in clique size, unlike standard NP-hardness reductions).

The paper establishes a unifying picture across several related problems (network verification, zonotope containment, Lipschitz constant computation) via the duality between positively homogeneous convex CPWL functions and polytopes/zonotopes, which is an elegant structural insight.

Results are accompanied by matching ETH-based lower bounds (ρ(d)·N^{o(d)} impossibility), showing that known brute-force enumeration algorithms are essentially optimal, which strengthens the significance of the hardness results beyond simple W[1]-hardness.

The paper also contributes some positive/tractability results (polynomial-time L1-Lipschitz and FPT L∞-Lipschitz for ICNNs, randomized FPT-approximation via subspace embeddings), rounding out the theoretical contribution with some constructive algorithmic content.
Writing is generally clear and well organized, with proof sketches in the main text and full proofs deferred to the appendix, and illustrative figures aid understanding of the reduction gadgets.
weaknesses: The paper is purely theoretical with no experiments, implementation, or empirical validation of any kind, which may limit its immediate impact and appeal to a broad ML audience, even though this is explicitly acknowledged as a limitation by the authors.

The core technical contribution, while solid, is largely incremental: it extends/closes gaps in a very recent COLT'25 paper by the same essential community (reduction techniques, homogenization, duality arguments) rather than introducing fundamentally new tools; much of the heavy lifting reuses established machinery (Sidon sets, hyperplane arrangement enumeration, subspace embeddings) applied in a fairly direct manner.

The significance of the results to the broader ML/verification community is unclear in practice: W[1]-hardness w.r.t. input dimension mostly confirms what practitioners likely already suspected (verification does not become easy just because input dimension is small, if d still scales with problem structure), and the paper does not provide concrete guidance for practical mitigation beyond vague suggestions (special architectures, heuristics).

Several central claims rely on proof sketches in the main body, with full rigor deferred to a lengthy appendix; while this is a common venue norm, some of the proof sketches (e.g., for Theorem 6.2's Lipschitz hardness with delicate epsilon-scaling arguments) are hard to verify from the main text alone, raising reproducibility/verifiability concerns for readers not willing to parse the appendix in detail.

The relationship to and precise delta over the companion COLT'25 paper (Froese et al. 2025a/b) is somewhat conflated throughout; it would help to have a clearer, explicit table contrasting exactly which results were already known (NP-hardness, XP algorithms) versus the new W[1]-hardness/ETH lower bounds contributed here, since currently this requires careful reading to disentangle.

The most interesting open question (Lp-maximization on zonotopes for p in (1,∞)) remains unresolved, and the provided randomized approximation algorithm (Section 7) has worse worst-case running time than existing approaches (Shenmaier 2018), undercutting its practical or theoretical novelty as a standalone contribution.

The paper's scope is narrow (2- and 3-layer ReLU/maxout networks only), and while the authors argue hardness for 2/3-layer implies hardness for deeper networks via trivial identity layers, this means the deeper-network results add little beyond the base case, slightly inflating the apparent scope of contributions in the abstract/intro.

strengths: Resolves an explicitly stated open problem from Froese et al. (COLT '25) regarding the parameterized complexity of network verification and the Lipschitz constant, providing a definitive answer (W[1]-hardness) rather than partial progress.

The core reduction (from Multicolored Clique via Sidon-set-based spike and penalty gadgets) is elegant and reused effectively across a wide range of related problems: positivity, surjectivity, maximum approximation, zonotope (non-)containment, and Lipschitz constant computation/approximation for various p, demonstrating strong technical versatility.

The hardness results come with matching algorithmic upper bounds and ETH-based running time lower bounds, giving a essentially complete characterization of the runtime dependence on the input dimension d for several fundamental problems, which is a rare and valuable type of tight result in this area.

Connects neural network verification to classical computational geometry (zonotope containment) and control/robotics applications, broadening the significance of the contribution beyond the ML verification community.

Includes complementary positive results (polynomial-time L1-Lipschitz computation and FPT L∞-Lipschitz computation for ICNNs, plus a randomized FPT-approximation scheme for zonotope norm maximization via subspace embeddings), giving a fuller picture of the tractability landscape rather than only negative results.

Proofs are carefully structured with proof sketches in the main text and full detailed proofs in the appendix, including auxiliary lemmas (e.g., on Sidon sets, homogenization) that are reusable building blocks.
Clearly delineates remaining open questions (Lp-maximization for p in (1,∞), complexity of L0, whether positivity is in W[1]), showing good scholarly awareness of the problem landscape.
weaknesses: The paper is purely theoretical with no empirical validation; while reasonable for a complexity-theory contribution, it limits insight into how these worst-case hardness results manifest in practically trained networks.

The overall reduction framework builds heavily on the machinery and gadget style already introduced by Froese et al. (2025b), so while the extensions are nontrivial and resolve open questions, the core technique is an extension rather than a fundamentally new approach.

Some of the quantitative arguments (e.g., the epsilon-scaling analysis for the Lp-Lipschitz constant hardness) are quite intricate and dense, which may make independent verification by readers difficult without carefully working through the appendix.
Limited discussion of practical implications or how these hardness results should inform the design of practical verification heuristics beyond a brief general statement in the conclusion.

The related work section explicitly notes it is not a full literature review, which, combined with the narrow technical focus, may reduce accessibility for readers less familiar with this specific sub-area.
The central open problem of whether 2-layer ReLU positivity itself is in W[1] remains unresolved, so the parameterized complexity landscape, while much clarified, is not fully closed.

strengths: Resolves a well-known open problem posed by Froese et al. at COLT'25 regarding the parameterized complexity of ReLU network positivity/verification and zonotope containment, providing a definitive answer (W[ℓ−1]-hardness) rather than a partial result.

The paper is comprehensive: it establishes matching upper and lower bounds (via careful XP algorithms and ETH-based lower bounds) for an entire family of related problems — positivity, surjectivity, Lipschitz constant computation/approximation, zonotope containment, injectivity, and convexity checking — showing that simple brute-force enumeration is essentially optimal.

Technically inventive reduction machinery: the Sidon-set based encoding for Multicolored Clique reductions and the 'homogenization' technique to remove biases while preserving hardness are elegant and reusable across many of the paper's results.

Strong connections are drawn between depth of ReLU networks and levels of the W-hierarchy, which is conceptually interesting and could stimulate further cross-fertilization between parameterized complexity theory and deep learning theory.

The paper also contributes positive/tractability results (polynomial-time and FPT algorithms for ICNNs, a randomized FPT-approximation algorithm for norm maximization on zonotopes via subspace embeddings), giving a fuller picture rather than only hardness results.

Very careful and rigorous handling of running-time lower bounds, including a refined analysis (Section 9, Corollary 9.4) showing that even combined-parameter running times of the form N^{O(ℓ+d)} are ruled out under ETH, going beyond what a naive combination of the single-parameter results would give.

Good organizational aids (Table 1) summarizing the many results, and clear connections/comparisons made to prior and concurrent work (Froese et al. 2025b, Virmaux and Scaman 2018, Jordan and Dimakis 2020, and very recent concurrent papers on Lp-norm maximization).
weaknesses: Some of the results on Lp-Lipschitz/norm maximization for p ∈ (1,∞) overlap substantially with concurrent independent works (Cao et al., Das et al., Dewasurendra and Jayawardhana, all cited as forthcoming 2026 papers), somewhat diminishing the novelty/priority of that specific slice of results, though the paper's own p=2/∞ and general framework contributions remain distinct.

The central structural open question the paper itself highlights (whether ℓ-layer positivity parameterized by d is complete for W[ℓ−1], i.e., whether matching containment in W[ℓ−1] holds, not just W[P]) is left unresolved even for ℓ=2, so the parameterized complexity landscape is not fully closed despite the paper's strong hardness contributions.

The paper is extremely dense and technical with many nested constructions (spike/penalty functions, homogenization, digit-decomposition gadgets); while rigorous, this limits accessibility and makes independent verification of all details (there are many technical lemmas and multi-case proofs) time-consuming for reviewers/readers.

Purely theoretical contribution with no empirical component; while this is appropriate for the problem type, the practical implications for real-world verification tool design are only briefly and speculatively discussed in the conclusion (e.g., no concrete guidance on how to exploit structure in trained networks).

Some claims about tightness (e.g., 'essentially optimal' running times) rely on standard but strong assumptions (ETH) and asymptotic notions (o(·) definitions in Section 9) whose practical relevance for realistic network sizes is not discussed.

strengths: Directly resolves an explicitly stated open problem from COLT '25 (Froese et al.) regarding parameterized complexity of ReLU network positivity/verification and zonotope containment, which is a clear and verifiable contribution.

Provides a comprehensive and unified set of hardness results (W[l-1]-hardness w.r.t. input dimension d for positivity, surjectivity, and Lp-Lipschitz constant computation for all l>=2, plus complementary hardness w.r.t. depth l for constant d), giving a fairly complete picture of the parameterized landscape summarized clearly in Table 1.

The reductions are technically non-trivial: the core Multicolored Clique reduction using Sidon sets to encode both node and edge information within a fixed small input dimension is a clever and reusable gadget, and its extensions (homogenization technique to remove biases while preserving hardness, layer-stacking constructions for higher weft) are carefully executed.

Matching upper and lower bounds: the paper shows brute-force enumeration algorithms (running in n^{(l-1)d}) are essentially optimal under ETH, which is a strong and satisfying tightness result rather than just qualitative hardness.

Includes positive/tractability results (poly-time L1-Lipschitz constant and FPT L∞ for ICNNs, randomized FPT-approximation via subspace embeddings for zonotope norm maximization) that nicely complement the hardness results and show the authors explored the tractability boundary, not just negative results.

The paper is thorough in deriving many corollaries (convexity checking, injectivity, function representability across depths) from the core constructions, extracting substantial mileage from the main technical machinery.
weaknesses: Several of the Lp-Lipschitz/zonotope-norm-maximization hardness results overlap with contemporaneous independent work (Cao et al. 2026, Dewasurendra and Jayawardhana 2026, Das et al. 2026), which somewhat dilutes the exclusivity/novelty of that portion of the contribution, even though the paper is transparent about this.

The central conjecture motivating the work (whether l-layer ReLU Positivity parameterized by d is W[l-1]-complete) is left open; even the base case (2-layer case) is not resolved between W[1]-hardness and W[P]-containment, so the paper's classification of the 'ReLU hierarchy' within the W-hierarchy is incomplete despite the title's framing.

The paper is purely theoretical/worst-case in nature with no empirical or practical validation of how these hardness results manifest for realistic trained networks; the practical implications remain speculative (the conclusion admits it is unclear which structural assumptions would let practitioners avoid the hardness).

The presentation is extremely dense with many nested technical gadgets (spike functions, penalty functions, homogenization, digit-decoding constructions) that, while rigorous, make the paper difficult to verify or appreciate without very careful line-by-line reading, limiting accessibility to a broad AI audience.

Some of the construction machinery (e.g., the spike/penalty gadget) is a direct extension of techniques already used in prior work (Froese et al. 2025b) for the simpler complexity classes, so part of the contribution is incremental engineering of existing gadget ideas to reach higher levels of the W-hierarchy rather than fundamentally new techniques.

strengths: Resolves a well-known open problem from COLT'25 regarding the parameterized complexity of ReLU network positivity/verification, providing a definitive answer (W[ℓ-1]-hardness) rather than a partial result.

Extremely comprehensive treatment: the paper simultaneously settles parameterized complexity (w.r.t. both input dimension d and depth ℓ) for positivity, surjectivity, injectivity, zonotope containment, Lipschitz constant computation/approximation, and convexity/equivalence-checking problems, with matching upper bounds via careful algorithmic analysis (Section 3) and a unified 'Table 1' summary.

Technically strong and inventive reductions: the Sidon-set based encoding for Multicolored Clique into 2-layer ReLU positivity (Prop. 4.1) is elegant and reused as the technical backbone for multiple hardness results; the 'homogenization' construction (Def. 5.1, Lemma 5.2) to remove biases while preserving hardness is a clean and non-trivial technical device.

Results are tight: the paper does not merely show NP/W-hardness but derives matching ETH-based running-time lower bounds (e.g., n^Ω(d)·poly(N)) that exactly match the brute-force enumeration algorithms, and even proves a refined lower bound on the joint parameter (ℓ+d) that rules out algorithms with runtime N^O(ℓ+d) (Corollary 9.4), going beyond what a naive combination of the two single-parameter results would give.

Good scope beyond pure hardness: the paper also gives positive/tractability results (P-time and FPT algorithms for L1/L∞-Lipschitz constant on ICNNs, a randomized FPT-approximation via subspace embeddings for zonotope norm maximization), giving a more complete picture rather than only negative results.

Establishes a novel conceptual bridge between the W-hierarchy (weft-bounded circuits) and bounded-depth ReLU networks, which could be of independent interest to the parameterized complexity community and stimulate further work.

Clear positioning relative to very recent independent related work (Cao et al. 2026, Das et al. 2026, Dewasurendra and Jayawardhana 2026) on Lp-norm maximization over zonotopes, showing the authors are aware of and appropriately credit concurrent developments.
weaknesses: The paper is entirely theoretical with no empirical component; while this is appropriate for a hardness/complexity paper, the practical implications discussed in the conclusion (e.g., regarding sparse/small weights not helping) are somewhat speculative and not empirically substantiated.

Several natural open questions remain unresolved by the paper itself and are only discussed in the conclusion (e.g., whether 2-layer ReLU Positivity parameterized by d is complete for W[1] rather than merely contained in W[P]; whether the 3-layer case is even in W[P]); the paper thus does not fully close the 'ReLU-hierarchy vs W-hierarchy' correspondence it proposes as its main conceptual contribution.

The presentation is very dense and technical, with long proofs relying on intricate piecewise-linear gadget constructions (penalty/spike functions, digit-decomposition networks) that, while rigorous, may be difficult for non-specialist readers to verify or appreciate without significant effort; a higher-level proof roadmap or more intuition in the main text (beyond figures) would improve accessibility.

Some of the individual hardness results (e.g., W[1]-hardness of Lp-norm maximization on zonotopes) have been superseded/paralleled by concurrent independent work cited in the paper, which somewhat dilutes the novelty of that specific sub-result, though the paper's broader scope (arbitrary ℓ, multiple problems, tight ETH bounds) still exceeds these concurrent papers.

The significance of the results is primarily of theoretical/foundational interest to the parameterized complexity and neural network verification theory community; the practical impact on real-world verification tool design is left largely as future work rather than demonstrated.
